`Cc1nc2ccc(-c3ccc([C@H](C)N4CC[C@](CC(C)(C)O)(c5ccccc5)OC4=O)cc3)cc2[nH]1`

This contains an indazole core (`[nH]1` and `c1`, `c2`).
There is a methyl group on the indazole ring (`Cc1`).
At position 5 (or similar), there is a phenyl ring attached: `-c3ccc(...)cc3`.
On this phenyl ring, there is a chiral center `[C@H](C)` attached to a nitrogen in a lactam ring: `N4CC[C@](CC(C)(C)O)(c5ccccc5)OC4=O`.
Wait, let's parse the lactam part carefully:
`N4CC[C@](CC(C)(C)O)(c5ccccc5)OC4=O`
This looks like a morpholinone or piperidinone derivative? No, it's a 6-membered ring with N, C, C, C(Quaternary), O, C=O. Wait, `N4CC[C@](...)OC4=O` means N-C-C-C(quat)-O-C(=O)-N. That's a morpholin-3-one derivative!
Actually, `N4CC[C@](CC(C)(C)O)(c5ccccc5)OC4=O` corresponds to a 3-morpholinone ring.
The quaternary carbon has a phenyl group (`c5ccccc5`) and a hydroxyisopropyl group (`CC(C)(C)O`).
Wait, `CC(C)(C)O` is a tert-butanol group attached via a CH2? No, `CC(C)(C)O` means `CH2-C(CH3)2-OH`. So it's a 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropyl group.
And the chiral center `[C@H](C)` connects the phenyl ring to the N of the morpholinone.

So the product is an indazole connected to a phenyl ring, which is connected to a chiral ethyl group, which is connected to a morpholinone nitrogen. The morpholinone has a phenyl and a hydroxyisopropyl group at the 3-position.
